passage: When an old building is to be repaired, those responsible must first decide what, exactly, they are repairing it to. One answer, long popular and still widely held, is that the building should be returned to its original state, or to the state its first builders intended. Later additions are stripped away, missing parts are reconstructed from evidence or from informed guesses, and the result is a building more complete and more consistent than it has been for centuries. The appeal is obvious: the visitor sees the church or the fort as it was meant to be seen, whole and coherent.

The opposing answer holds that a building's history does not stop at its completion. A medieval hall that later acquired a Georgian window, a Victorian staircase and a twentieth-century kitchen is a document of all those periods, and to strip it back to its first state is to erase most of what it records. On this view the repairer's duty is to keep what has survived, to intervene as little as possible, and to make any new work distinguishable from the old, so that no one mistakes a modern guess for an original fact. The restored building, by contrast, presents the restorer's idea of the past as though it were the past itself.

I find the second answer more persuasive, but it is not as neutral as its defenders sometimes suggest. Not every layer is worth keeping: a cheap partition put up in a hurry may hide a painted ceiling of real importance, and refusing to remove it is itself a choice about which history matters. Keeping everything is also an interpretation, one that values continuity over quality and treats the accident of survival as a kind of verdict. The conservator, no less than the restorer, decides what the building will say.

What separates the two approaches, then, is not that one interprets and the other does not. It is that conservation, at its best, leaves its interpretations visible and reversible, so that a later generation with better evidence or different priorities can undo them. Restoration tends to make its choices permanent and to conceal them, since a convincing reconstruction is one in which the seams cannot be found. Because every generation has been confident about the past and most have been wrong about some of it, the approach that allows its mistakes to be corrected deserves the benefit of the doubt.

passage: Every entrenched constitution invites an awkward question. If a majority of citizens today wishes to change some arrangement, why should it be prevented from doing so by rules that were drafted generations ago by people who are now dead, and who could not have imagined the conditions under which their successors live? A requirement that amendments win two-thirds of the legislature, or the approval of most regions, looks from this angle like a device for letting the past outvote the present. The objection has a democratic edge that is hard to dismiss: it asks by what right one generation sets the terms on which another must govern itself. Nor is it answered by praising the wisdom of the framers, since wisdom about one century is no warrant for authority over the next.

The most familiar answer appeals to self-binding. Just as a sailor who knows he will be tempted by a dangerous song may order his crew to tie him to the mast and ignore his later pleas, a people may bind itself in a calm moment against the passions it expects to feel in an agitated one. Entrenchment, on this account, is not the past overruling the present but the present protecting itself from its own worst impulses. The image is attractive, but it does not fit the case. The sailor binds himself, and the man who later strains at the ropes is the same man who gave the order. A constitution binds people who were not present when it was adopted and who gave no order at all. To call this self-binding is to assume precisely the continuity of the collective self that the objection calls into question.

A better defence starts from a different picture of what entrenchment does. Amendment rules do not, in practice, pit the living against the dead, because the dead cast no votes. What such rules do is set the terms on which living citizens must settle disagreements among themselves. When an amendment fails for want of a supermajority, it is defeated not by its framers but by a present minority large enough to block it. The requirement thus protects groups that might otherwise be outvoted on matters basic to their standing, and it encourages proposals that can attract support beyond a single faction. The protection is not merely theoretical: a group that knows it can block changes to its basic standing has less reason to fear the ordinary swings of electoral fortune, and more reason to accept defeat on everything else. Seen this way, the hand that restrains the majority is a living hand, and the real question is whether present minorities deserve such a veto, not whether the past deserves obedience.

This reframing does not make the original worry vanish. It succeeds only where amendment is demanding but genuinely possible. A constitution whose amendment procedure is so onerous that no change has been achieved in living memory, or which declares certain provisions unamendable altogether, really does impose the judgement of its authors on everyone who comes after; there, no present coalition, however broad, can alter the text. The objection from the dead hand is therefore best understood not as a refutation of entrenchment as such but as a warning about its extremes. Between a constitution that any passing majority may rewrite and one that no one can, the useful argument concerns how much agreement change should require, and that is a question each generation is entitled to keep asking.

passage: Whenever a machine produces fluent language, the question returns of whether it understands what it says. Two answers dominate. One holds that understanding is shown in behaviour: if a system answers questions, follows instructions and sustains a conversation in ways we cannot distinguish from a competent person, there is nothing further we could reasonably ask of it, and to withhold the word is mere prejudice in favour of our own kind. The other holds that behaviour, however impressive, can be produced by manipulating symbols whose connection to the world the system never grasps, and that understanding requires something behind the performance, some grounding of words in perception, action or experience.

The two camps disagree about almost everything except one assumption, and that shared assumption is where the trouble lies. Both treat understanding as a single property that a system either has or lacks, so that the only task is to decide which side of the line it falls on. Yet when we attribute understanding to people we do nothing of the kind. A student may understand a theorem well enough to apply it to textbook problems but not well enough to see why it fails when one condition is dropped; a mechanic may understand an engine thoroughly in practice while being unable to explain its thermodynamics. We judge understanding by a battery of loosely connected abilities: explaining, extending to unfamiliar cases, noticing one's own mistakes, connecting what one knows to what one does. These abilities can come apart, and people possess them in very different measures.

If understanding is a cluster of this kind, the all-or-nothing question about machines is badly posed. A system may display some of the abilities to a high degree and others hardly at all; it may extend a pattern brilliantly in one domain and fail, without any sign of noticing, at a trivial variation in another. Saying that it 'really understands' flattens this profile into a verdict that tells us little, and saying that it 'merely manipulates symbols' does the same in the opposite direction. The useful work lies in mapping which abilities are present, under what conditions, and how robustly.

This proposal will not satisfy everyone. Someone who believes that understanding involves an inner experience of meaning will say that mapping abilities, however finely, leaves the essential question untouched. Perhaps it does. But that question, whatever its answer, is a question about experience, and it arises equally for any being whose inner life we cannot inspect. It should not be allowed to stand in for the more tractable question of what a system can and cannot reliably do, which is, after all, the question on which most practical decisions about such systems depend.

passage: In most markets the price does the work of allocation. If more people want a good than there are units of it, the price rises until the excess disappears, and whoever is willing to pay the new price obtains the good. But there is a family of markets in which this mechanism cannot operate, because each side must choose the other. A university cannot simply admit whoever is willing to pay the most, nor can an applicant simply buy a place; a hospital hiring junior doctors cares which doctors it gets, and the doctors care which hospital they join. In such markets, sometimes called matching markets, a transaction requires mutual acceptance, and no single number can bring about a match that both sides want.

Left to themselves, matching markets tend to fail in characteristic ways. One is unravelling: because the strongest candidates are in demand, employers try to secure them by making offers earlier than their rivals, and the competition for earliness can push offers so far forward that they are made before anyone knows how good the candidates are. Another is congestion: when offers must be accepted or refused quickly, a candidate holding one offer may not learn in time of a better one, and the market clears without having considered all its possibilities. A third is strategic misrepresentation, in which participants conceal their true preferences, ranking a likely option first rather than the one they actually want, because they fear that revealing their real wishes will cost them.

The remedy that has often been adopted is not deregulation but construction: a clearinghouse to which both sides submit ranked lists, and which computes an assignment by a procedure known to have certain properties. The property most often sought is stability, meaning that there is no applicant and employer, not matched to each other, who would both prefer to be. A stable assignment removes the motive to break ranks, since no such pair can do better by striking a private deal, and with a suitable procedure at least one side can be given no reason to misreport its preferences. Such clearinghouses show that a market is not always a spontaneous order arising wherever people are free to trade; it can be an artefact, built to solve problems that freedom alone creates.

None of this means that design can substitute for the willingness of participants. A clearinghouse works only if enough of both sides join it, and an elegant procedure is useless if the most sought-after employers find it more profitable to recruit privately. Nor can a procedure deliver every desirable property at once: no procedure, for instance, can give both sides complete reason to report honestly while always producing stable outcomes. The designer chooses among imperfect options, and the choice reflects judgements about whose interests deserve protection. The engineering of markets is thus a political as well as a technical art, but it is an art that can be practised well or badly, and the difference matters to the people whose lives it arranges.

passage: Few things in a museum are read as often, or looked at as little, as the wall label. Visitors approaching a painting frequently read the small panel beside it first, glance at the picture to confirm what they have been told, and move on. Curators have noticed this pattern for a long time, and it has produced two opposite reactions. One camp argues that labels should be shortened or removed altogether, so that the visitor is thrown back onto the object. The other argues that labels should be expanded, written in friendlier language and supplemented with audio guides and screens, since a public that does not know what it is looking at cannot be expected to care.

Both reactions treat the label as though its only variable were quantity. The purist assumes that less text means more looking, but a visitor confronted by an unexplained altarpiece does not usually begin to look harder; more often she feels excluded and walks faster. The expansionist assumes that more text means more understanding, yet a long label that rehearses the artist's biography, the patron's family and the painting's later owners gives the visitor a great deal to know and very little to see. In each case the label is imagined as a container of facts, and the only argument is over how full the container should be.

A better question is what the label asks the visitor to do. A label can close a picture, by telling the viewer what it means, or it can open it, by directing attention to something that can be checked against the canvas itself. Compare two sentences about the same imagined portrait. The first says that the sitter was a wealthy merchant who commissioned the work to celebrate his marriage. The second says that the merchant's left hand rests on a ledger while his right holds his wife's glove, and invites the reader to decide which hand the painter has lit more brightly. The first sentence can be absorbed without raising one's eyes; the second cannot be finished without looking.

None of this means that historical information is a distraction. A viewer who does not know that a certain blue, ground from a semi-precious stone, was once among the costliest materials a painter could buy will miss part of what a patron was displaying when he asked for a sky full of it, and no amount of attentive looking will supply that fact. The point is that information earns its place on the wall when it changes what the visitor notices. Facts that merely sit beside the object, however accurate, belong in the catalogue, where they can be read at leisure by those who want them. The wall is too valuable, and the visitor's attention too brief, to be spent on anything else.

passage: It is often said that overconfidence is the most pervasive of the biases, the one from which many of the others draw their strength. The claim is repeated so often that it is easy to miss how much it conceals. 'Overconfidence' names at least three different things, and they do not always travel together. Treating them as one has made the phenomenon seem both more universal and more mysterious than it is.

The first is overestimation: believing that one has performed, or will perform, better than one actually does. The second is overplacement: believing that one is better than other people. The third, which receives less public attention, is overprecision: excessive certainty that one's beliefs are accurate, shown when people asked for a range they are ninety per cent sure contains some true value give ranges that contain it far less often than that. These sound like variations on a single vanity, but they come apart in revealing ways. On tasks that are easy, people tend to underestimate how well they have done, even as they place themselves above others; on tasks that are very hard, the pattern reverses, and many people will rate themselves below average at, say, juggling or composing verse while still overestimating their own scores.

What explains such reversals is less a desire to think well of oneself than the way information is distributed. People usually know more about their own performance than about other people's, so their judgements of others are pulled toward a vague middle. When a task is hard, they correctly sense that they did poorly but assume that others did less badly; when it is easy, the opposite. A good deal of what looks like ego, in other words, is a predictable consequence of reasoning from imperfect information about the people with whom one is being compared.

Overprecision is different. It shows no comparable tendency to reverse, appearing on easy and hard questions, among novices and among specialists, and it is the form that does most harm in planning, where projects are budgeted against ranges too narrow to include what actually happens. It is also the form that most resists exhortation: telling forecasters to be humble rarely widens their intervals much. More promising are procedures that change the question, such as asking people to assign probabilities to several ranges in turn, so that the possibility of an outcome far from their best guess must be considered explicitly rather than waved away. The lesson is not that confidence is good or bad but that a single word has been doing the work of three, and that each of the three needs its own diagnosis.

options.B: give much wider ranges for their estimates than they do on easy tasks, so that their overprecision disappears.
options.C: rate themselves above average compared with others while underestimating how well they have actually done.
options.D: rate themselves below average compared with others while still overestimating their own scores.

passage: The doctrine that a territory could be treated as belonging to no one, terra nullius, is often described as a lie that settlers told themselves. The lands of Australia or North America, the argument runs, were plainly inhabited; to declare them empty was either a culpable ignorance or a convenient fiction, and once the facts are acknowledged the doctrine collapses. There is something right in this, but it misdescribes the doctrine's real strength. Most of the people who invoked the idea of empty land were perfectly aware that others lived there. What they denied was not presence but a particular kind of relationship to the land, one that their own law was prepared to recognise as ownership.

The intellectual resources for that denial were readily available. An influential strand of early modern European thought held that property arose when a person mixed his labour with the earth, enclosing it, ploughing it and improving it; John Locke's well-known version of the argument drew explicitly on the example of America. On this view, land that was hunted over, gathered from, burned to renew its grasses or moved across with the seasons had not yet been appropriated, however long people had lived on it. The settlers' error, if it was one, was not a failure to see but a theory of what was worth seeing. Fences, fields and permanent buildings registered as use; songs that mapped water sources, rules governing who might hunt where, and the careful management of fire did not.

This matters because the doctrine has now been formally repudiated in several places, most famously when the High Court of Australia in 1992 rejected the proposition that the continent had belonged to no one at the time of British settlement, a proposition on which much of the country's land law had quietly rested. The repudiation was a real achievement, and it would be ungracious to belittle it. Yet the regimes of native title that followed typically require claimants to show that they have maintained a continuing connection with the land under traditional laws and customs, often to the satisfaction of courts that weigh written records and documented occupation heavily. Communities that were driven off their country, or whose practices were suppressed, find that the very dispossession they complain of becomes evidence against them: a broken connection, however it was broken, is a weaker claim.

In other words, the factual premise of terra nullius has been abandoned while something like its theoretical premise survives. Title still depends on displaying a relationship to land in forms that a court is equipped to recognise, and the forms most easily recognised are those that leave records. The burden has simply been reversed. Where the settler state once declared the land empty and left the inhabitants to prove otherwise in practice, the modern claimant must now prove, in a forum designed by the settler state, that the land was never emptied of them.

It does not follow that recognition is worthless, or that some purer form of restitution is readily available. Any legal system must have rules of proof, and claims that could be made without evidence would invite abuse. The point is narrower. A doctrine is not fully dismantled when its conclusion is reversed if the standard used to apply the reversal was shaped by the doctrine itself. To finish the work would require asking not only whether people were present, which no one now denies, but whose ways of being present count as having a place.

passage: Two attitudes to the character of the speaker run through the study of persuasion, and they are hard to reconcile. The first, familiar from introductory logic, holds that an argument stands or falls on its own terms. Who makes it is irrelevant; to reject a claim because of the person advancing it is to commit a fallacy, and to accept a claim because of the person is the same error in a friendlier mood. The second attitude is older. Aristotle counted the character of the speaker among the means of persuasion, alongside appeals to the emotions of the audience and to the argument itself, and he did not present it as a regrettable weakness of listeners. A speaker who seems sensible, honest and well disposed towards the audience is, on this view, more worthy of belief, and an audience is right to take that into account.

The logician's attitude is correct for a particular situation: one in which the listener can examine the argument fully. A proof in geometry is no better for coming from a famous mathematician. But most of the claims on which people must act are not like proofs. A patient cannot check a diagnosis, a juror cannot repeat the forensic analysis, and a citizen cannot audit the statistics behind a policy. In such cases the listener is not choosing between evaluating the argument and evaluating the speaker; the argument is largely out of reach, and the speaker's record, competence and incentives are the best evidence available. To attend to them is not a lapse in reasoning but reasoning under a division of intellectual labour that no one can escape.

If this rehabilitates the appeal to character, it also shows where that appeal goes wrong. Credibility is earned in a domain. The physician's record is evidence about diagnoses, not about tax policy, and the honesty of a popular broadcaster is evidence that he reports what he believes, not that what he believes is true. Much modern persuasion works by carrying trust from the place where it was earned to a place where it has no bearing: the athlete who recommends an investment, the scientist who pronounces on matters far from her field. The listener who accepts such claims is not wrong to rely on character in general; she is wrong about which character she is relying on.

The two attitudes, then, are less opposed than they first appear. The logician is right that character cannot make a bad argument good, and the rhetorician is right that, where arguments cannot be inspected, character is often all a listener has to go on. What a careful audience needs is neither a rule against attending to the speaker nor a habit of trusting the likeable, but the narrower discipline of asking what, exactly, the speaker's credibility is credibility about.

passage: A great deal of advertising tells the viewer almost nothing. A television spot in which a famous athlete drinks a soft drink on a beach conveys no fact about the drink's price, ingredients or taste that a sceptical viewer could check, and critics of advertising have long drawn what seems the obvious conclusion: if the message carries no information, the money spent on it is either wasted or devoted to manipulation, persuading people to want things by associating them with glamour. The conclusion is natural, but it rests on the assumption that whatever an advertisement communicates must be contained in what it says or shows, and that assumption is open to question.

Consider the matter from the firm's side. A company launching a product that is cheap to try, such as a breakfast cereal or a shampoo, makes its money not from the first purchase but from the repeat purchases of customers who liked it. A firm confident that its product is good therefore expects a long stream of returns from anyone it persuades to try it once, whereas a firm that knows its product is mediocre expects most of those who try it never to return. Lavish advertising is accordingly worth far more to the first firm than to the second, and a consumer who sees a product advertised extravagantly may reasonably infer that its maker is wagering on repeat business. On this view the expense of the advertisement is itself the message, and the athlete and the beach matter chiefly because everyone can see that they cost a fortune.

The argument has real force, but its reach is limited. It applies most clearly to what economists call experience goods, whose quality can be judged only after use, and only where repeat purchase is likely; a firm selling something that people buy once in a lifetime gains little from the signal, because satisfied customers will not return in any case. For goods whose qualities can be inspected before purchase, such as the dimensions of a table or the fare for a train journey, advertising informs directly and requires no signalling story at all. Nor does the argument show that every extravagant campaign is a reliable signal, since a firm may overspend from vanity or miscalculation, and imitators may learn to mimic the outward appearance of expense more cheaply than it seems.

A familiar objection is that ordinary consumers do not reason in this way, since nobody watching a soft drink advertisement contemplates the economics of repeat purchase. The objection misunderstands what the argument requires. Consumers need not reconstruct the logic; it is enough that they follow a rule of thumb, such as trusting brands they have heard of, and that the rule tends, on the whole, to reward them. The signalling account does not vindicate advertising, and it leaves the question of manipulation entirely open. What it does establish is that an advertisement without content is not, for that reason alone, an advertisement without meaning.

passage: Debt is described, almost everywhere, in moral vocabulary. We speak of honouring our debts and of meeting our obligations, while default is treated as a failure of character and the borrower who cannot pay is presumed to have been improvident. These words are old, and they carry the experience of every society that has had to persuade strangers to trust one another across time. The language is not wholly misplaced, since a promise to repay is a promise, and a society in which such promises were lightly broken would soon find that no one would lend at all.

The moral framing, however, assigns the whole of the responsibility to one side of what is a two-sided contract. A loan is made by a lender who chose to lend, who estimated the chance of not being repaid and built that chance into the rate of interest, and who has been paid, in that higher rate, for bearing exactly the risk that sometimes comes to pass. When a borrower defaults, the risk for which the lender was compensated has simply materialised. To treat default as a sin rather than as an outcome the contract foresaw is to let lenders collect the premium for risk while disowning the risk itself.

This asymmetry has practical consequences. Where the moral framing is strong, lenders come under less pressure to judge carefully whether a borrower can repay, since any failure will be laid at the borrower's door, and borrowers in difficulty may conceal their distress out of shame instead of seeking to renegotiate early, when a settlement would cost both parties least. A lender that knows blame will travel in only one direction has in effect been relieved of part of the cost of its own mistakes, and an institution relieved of that cost can be expected to make more of them. The bankruptcy law of many countries embodies a different view: it treats a fresh start for an honest debtor as a social good, partly on the practical ground that a person crushed by debts that can never be paid produces little for anyone, creditors included.

None of this licenses casual default, and a borrower who spends money he never meant to return has done wrong in the plainest sense. The point is that obligation runs in both directions: the borrower owes repayment, and the lender owes care in deciding to lend. A moral language that recognised both duties would not be softer than the one we have; it would simply be more accurate about where responsibility lies when a loan goes bad.

passage: When people imagine an intelligent animal, they usually imagine something built on the plan of their own bodies: a large brain in the head that gathers information, makes decisions and issues commands to obedient limbs. The octopus is a standing challenge to that picture. Its evolutionary line separated from ours more than half a billion years ago, long before either lineage had anything resembling a complex brain, so whatever intelligence it now has was assembled independently. And it was assembled on a strikingly different plan, for more of the octopus's neurons lie in its arms than in its central brain.

The arrangement has consequences that can be observed. An octopus arm can carry out a sequence of movements, such as reaching towards an object and bending to draw it in, with little apparent direction from the centre, and an arm separated from the body will for a time continue to respond to touch and to grasp what it meets. Each arm, it seems, handles much of the detail of its own movement, while the central brain sets broader goals. Instead of a commander and its troops, the better image might be a coordinator working with partners that each know their own business.

Popular writing has been quick to turn this into a slogan, describing the octopus as an animal with nine brains, or as a colony of minds sharing one body. The slogan goes too far. The arms are not independent agents with purposes of their own; they share a body, a nervous system and, in ordinary life, a single course of action, and the animal behaves as one creature pursuing one end at a time. What the anatomy shows is not that the octopus is many minds but that one mind can be organised so that much of its work is done at the edges.

That is the real lesson, and it reaches beyond octopuses. Much thinking about intelligence, in animals and in machines alike, has assumed that it must be centralised: that there must be some single place where everything comes together and is decided. The octopus suggests that centralisation is one solution among several, suited to some bodies and not to others. An animal with eight flexible arms and no skeleton faces a control problem that no single centre could easily solve, since each arm can bend at any point along its length and in any direction. Handing much of the work to the arms may be less an evolutionary curiosity than a sensible answer to the body the animal actually has.

passage: When two researchers, one celebrated and one unknown, publish a discovery together, the discovery is very likely to be remembered as the celebrated researcher's. The same pattern appears when two people arrive at a result independently: the one who is already eminent tends to receive the larger share of the attention, the citations and the invitations that follow. Sociologists of science named this the Matthew effect, after the verse in the Gospel of Matthew about those who have being given more, and it is usually discussed as a problem of fairness. The unknown co-author did much of the work, and someone else collected the credit.

That description is correct within its limits, but it understates what is at stake, and it also misses why the effect is so persistent. Scientists face a literature far larger than anyone could read in a lifetime. A familiar name on a paper is a cheap signal that the paper is probably worth the reader's time, and in a world of scarce attention, readers who rely on such signals are not being foolish. To some degree, then, the effect is the by-product of a reasonable strategy for coping with abundance. Condemning it as mere snobbery does not explain why careful and fair-minded people take part in it every day.

The trouble begins when attention is converted into resources. A researcher whose papers are widely read finds it easier to win grants, which pay for students and equipment, which produce more papers, which are read more widely still. Advantage compounds. After a few rounds, the difference between two careers may bear little relation to any difference in the quality of their first ideas, and the field as a whole has placed a heavy bet on one line of work for reasons that are partly accidental. Ideas that happened to originate with the less visible researcher may wait years for a hearing, or never receive one, not because they were tested and found wanting but because nobody with the means to test them was looking in their direction.

Seen in this light, the effect is less an injustice done to individuals than a distortion in how a field allocates its bets, and the remedy is not to forbid readers from noticing names, which would be both futile and costly. It is to loosen the link between attention and money: to judge some grant proposals without knowing who wrote them, to set aside funds for researchers early in their careers, and to treat a famous name as a reason to read a paper rather than as a reason to believe it.

passage: Archives were not assembled to answer the questions historians now put to them. A colonial archive records what an administration needed to know: revenue collected and revenue owed, disorders suppressed, petitions received and disposed of. The people it governed appear in its pages chiefly at the moments when they became a problem for the state, as defaulters, suspects, rebels or supplicants. A historian who reads such records along the grain, accepting their categories as descriptions of reality, will end up reproducing the administration's own view of the world, in which a refusal to pay becomes 'obstinacy' and a gathering at a shrine becomes a 'disturbance of the peace'.

The remedy most often proposed is to read against the grain: to treat the record as evidence of what it was designed to suppress or dismiss. A report that a village had refused its dues 'without any cause' can be read for the cause the clerk declined to set down. The insistence of officials, repeated across a dozen letters, that a rumour was baseless tells us that the rumour mattered a great deal to them, and probably to those who spread it. Fear, in such documents, is a kind of evidence. Practised with care, this method has produced some of the most illuminating social history of recent generations, restoring motive and intelligence to people whom the record had reduced to nuisances.

Yet the method has a limit that its enthusiasts sometimes forget. Reading against the grain still reads the grain. The voices it recovers belong to those who left a trace by colliding with power; those who never collided, who paid what was asked, married, worked their fields and died without incident, remain exactly where the archive left them, outside it. There is also a quieter temptation. When the record is thin, the historian's sympathies rush in to fill it, and the rebel recovered from the margins of an official report can look suspiciously like the rebel the historian set out hoping to find.

None of this is a reason to abandon the method. It is a reason to be candid about what it can and cannot do. A silence in the archive is not always a hidden voice waiting to be decoded; sometimes it is simply an absence, and the honest response is to mark it as one. Beyond that, the historian can turn to sources that were not produced by the same gaze: remembered songs and stories, the remains of houses and tools, the shape of fields and paths. The archive can be cross-examined with great profit, but it cannot be made to testify about what it never saw.

passage: Every alliance contains a quiet bargain between two fears. A state that joins an alliance worries, on the one hand, that its partner will fail it when it is attacked: this is the fear of abandonment. It worries, on the other, that its partner will drag it into a war it has no wish to fight, over interests that are not its own: this is the fear of entrapment. The two fears pull in opposite directions, and much of what passes for the routine management of alliances, the ministerial visits, the joint statements, the careful wording of guarantees, is an effort to keep them in tolerable balance.

The difficulty is that almost anything done to ease one fear aggravates the other. A state that tightens its commitment, by stationing troops on its partner's soil or promising automatic assistance, reassures the partner that it will not be abandoned. But the same assurance may embolden the partner to take risks it would otherwise avoid, confident that its ally will be obliged to follow. Loosening the commitment has the opposite effect: it restrains the partner, but it also invites the partner to doubt the alliance and perhaps to look for other friends, or to arm in ways that alarm its neighbours. There is no setting of the dial at which both fears disappear, and governments that search for one tend to lurch between them, reassuring an anxious ally one year and reining in an emboldened one the next.

For this reason, the ambiguity of many alliance commitments, often criticised as a failure of nerve, is better seen as a deliberate instrument. A guarantee that is firm enough to deter an adversary but vague about the circumstances in which it will be honoured leaves the protecting power room to judge whether its partner has provoked the crisis. The partner, uncertain whether reckless conduct will be supported, has reason to be careful; the adversary, uncertain whether aggression will be resisted, has reason to be careful too. Consider a hypothetical great power that promises to defend an island partner but declines to say whether the promise covers a dispute the partner itself might start. The silence is not an oversight. It is the policy.

The balance between the two fears is rarely the same for both members. A small state facing a powerful neighbour usually fears abandonment far more than entrapment, since it has few other places to turn, while its larger protector, with interests elsewhere and wars it would prefer not to fight, tends to fear entrapment more. Much of the friction within alliances that look harmonious from outside comes from this asymmetry: the junior partner asks for firmer pledges, the senior partner resists giving them, and each suspects the other of bad faith when each is in fact responding sensibly to its own position.

Ambiguity is not free, however. Its value depends on each party reading the uncertainty in the way the protecting power intends, and there is no guarantee that they will. An adversary may conclude that a vague commitment is a hollow one and test it, discovering too late that it was real. A partner may conclude that it will be supported whatever it does, because it cannot imagine its patron allowing it to fall. Deliberate vagueness thus trades the visible risks of a firm commitment for the hidden risk of miscalculation, which is the more dangerous for being invisible until a crisis reveals it. The strategy rewards a protecting power that understands both its partner and its adversary well, and punishes one that merely hopes it does.

passage: Few settlement forms have been as consistently disparaged by writers as the suburb. For the better part of a century, novelists, critics and social scientists have described it in a nearly fixed vocabulary: monotonous rows of identical houses, lawns tended out of anxiety rather than pleasure, a life of commuting, shopping and television in which neighbours are near but never known. The suburb, in this account, is where individuality goes to be smoothed away. The striking thing about the indictment is not its severity but its uniformity, which ought to make us suspicious. A form of life chosen by many millions of households can hardly be as simple as the language used to dismiss it.

Part of the indictment is sound. A district built around the car leaves those who cannot drive, the young, the old and the poor, stranded in a landscape in which nothing is within reach on foot. Zoning that separates homes from shops and workplaces by law multiplies journeys and empties the streets of the casual traffic through which neighbours become familiar. These are real costs, and they fall unevenly. But they are the costs of particular design decisions, and the critique of the suburb has rarely been content to remain at that level.

Its deeper charge is cultural, and here it is weakest. It reads sameness of form as sameness of life, as if a street of similar houses must contain similar people living similar days; anyone who has knocked on the doors of such a street knows otherwise. It also tends to treat the wish for a garden, a quiet bedroom and a door one can close as a failure of imagination, when for families leaving cramped flats these were precisely the goods that city life had denied them. The critics, many of whom lived by choice in the centres of large cities, were often describing a preference they did not share as a pathology from which others suffered.

None of this requires us to admire the suburb, or to ignore the costs of a pattern of building that consumes land and fuel at a great rate. It requires only that criticism be aimed at what can be changed. The desire for privacy and space is not a defect to be corrected; the absence of a shop within walking distance is. A suburb with a small centre, mixed uses and streets that a child can safely cross would answer most of the sound objections without asking anyone to want a different life.

passage: 'I did not know' is among the oldest excuses there is, and often among the best. We do not blame a pharmacist who dispenses a medicine that was contaminated at the factory in a way no inspection could detect, nor a traveller who carries a parcel for a friend without any reason to suspect what it contains. In such cases ignorance breaks the link between what a person did and what she intended, and blame that disregarded this would be blame for bad luck.

But the excuse has a counterfeit form. Consider a manager who tells his staff that he wants results and does not want to hear how they are achieved. When it later emerges that the results were achieved by falsifying safety records, he can say, truthfully, that he did not know. Yet his not knowing was not something that happened to him; it was something he arranged. He foresaw that there might be facts he would be obliged to act on, and he took steps to ensure that he would never be in possession of them. To accept his excuse would be to reward precisely the foresight that makes him responsible.

The distinction, then, is not between knowing and not knowing but between ignorance a person suffers and ignorance a person cultivates. The cultivated kind does not cancel responsibility; if anything, it adds a second fault to the first, since the person has both allowed a wrong to occur and taken care to shield himself from ever having to confront it. This is why such a person can seem, on reflection, no better and perhaps rather worse than someone who knew the facts plainly and still did nothing about them.

One should not push this too far. No one can investigate everything, and a demand that we trace the full history of every product we buy and every institution we deal with would be impossible to meet and would make ordinary life unworkable. Routine purchases, everyday dealings with banks and employers, and the countless small transactions of daily life proceed, quite properly, on the assumption that things are roughly as they appear. The charge of cultivated ignorance is fair only where a person had some particular reason to suspect a problem and chose not to look because looking might oblige him to act. Without such a reason, not inquiring is simply the normal condition of finite beings, and it is no more blameworthy than failing to read every book in a library.

passage: During the twentieth century a movement grew up among performers of European music written before about 1800 that sought to recover how that music had sounded when it was new. Its adherents played on instruments built to older designs, or on surviving originals: harpsichords rather than modern pianos, gut strings rather than steel, wooden flutes without the elaborate keywork of later models. They studied treatises on performance written in the period and drew from them conclusions about tempo, ornamentation and the size of ensembles. Much of the result was a revelation. Textures that had sounded thick and heavy when played by large modern orchestras became transparent, and pieces long heard as dutiful exercises began to sound witty and alive.

The difficulty lies in the word that the movement often attached to itself, authenticity. If authenticity means sounding as the music sounded to its first audiences, the goal is in one important respect unreachable. Even if every instrument and every tempo could be reconstructed exactly, the listeners could not be. An audience that has heard the music of the following two centuries hears an older piece against all of it; a dissonance that once startled may now pass unnoticed, and a small ensemble that once seemed ordinary may now sound austere and pointed. The same sounds, entering differently formed ears, do not produce the same experience.

A second difficulty concerns the composers' own wishes. It is sometimes assumed that a composer who wrote for the instruments of his day would have wanted exactly those instruments, and that a performance on them is therefore more faithful to his intentions. But composers wrote for what was available, and some of them are known to have been dissatisfied with the instruments and players they had. To infer a preference from a circumstance is to confuse what a composer was given with what he would have chosen.

None of this tells against the performances themselves, many of which are among the most vivid of the past century. It tells against a particular way of justifying them. The best of these performances persuade not because they are correct, in the sense of matching a lost original, but because the research behind them led performers to hear possibilities that habit had concealed. Historical evidence used in this way is less a rulebook than a provocation: a reason to try something, which must then succeed or fail as music.

passage: Why does a string quartet cost so much more to hear today, relative to a shirt or a radio, than it did a century ago? Not because the musicians have become greedy or the concert halls inefficient. Performing a quartet required four players and roughly forty minutes then, and it requires the same now; no innovation has allowed three musicians to play it in half the time without destroying the thing being bought. Meanwhile workers in manufacturing have become many times more productive, and their wages have risen accordingly. The musicians' pay must rise too, or they would drift into other work. So the price of the quartet climbs relative to goods whose production has been transformed, even though nothing about the quartet has changed.

Economists sometimes call this the cost disease, and its reach goes far beyond concert halls. Teaching, nursing, care of the elderly and much legal and administrative work share the quartet's structure: the service largely consists of a person's time and attention, and attempts to compress that time often degrade what is delivered. A class of sixty is cheaper per pupil than a class of thirty, but it is not the same product at a lower price. Where productivity in such sectors lags, their share of national spending rises, and with it a persistent suspicion that schools and hospitals are squandering money, since nearly everything else seems to be getting cheaper.

The diagnosis contains a consolation that is often missed. If the relative cost of services rises because the rest of the economy has become more productive, then society as a whole is richer, and can afford those services even at their higher relative price. A family that spends a larger share of its income on its children's schooling than its grandparents did may also own far more and work fewer hours. What feels like a crisis of affordability is, on this view, partly a change in the composition of a growing budget.

The argument should not be stretched into a blanket excuse. That some cost growth in services is unavoidable does not mean that all of it is; administrative layers can multiply in a hospital as easily as in any other organisation, and the cost disease offers them no defence. Nor is the consolation automatic. The higher relative price of care falls hardest on those whose incomes have not shared in the general gain, and public budgets that depend on taxes voters resist may cut services long before the arithmetic says they must. The cost disease explains a pattern; it does not settle who should pay for it.

passage: Moral philosophers argue with cases. A theory is proposed, someone describes a situation in which the theory delivers a verdict that strikes nearly everyone as monstrous, and the theory is revised or abandoned. The practice treats our considered reactions to cases, usually called intuitions, as something like data: not infallible, but weighty enough that a principle which contradicts too many of them loses its claim on us. Critics have long found this method suspicious. Intuitions, they point out, are the residue of upbringing, culture and evolutionary pressures that had nothing to do with tracking moral truth. To test theories against them is to test a map against the traveller's prejudices about where the roads ought to go.

The objection has force, but it proves less than it seems to. Every method of inquiry begins with some judgements it does not, at that moment, question; the empirical sciences rely on perceptual reports whose reliability can be checked only by further perception. The question is not whether intuitions have causes unrelated to truth, for every belief has causes, but whether we have specific reason to think a particular intuition distorted. Sometimes we do. An intuition that tracks a vivid feature of a case, such as whether harm is done with one's own hands, while ignoring features that on reflection seem to matter more, such as how much harm is done, earns suspicion. But suspicion of that kind is itself grounded in other intuitions, about which features matter and which do not.

This is why the familiar picture of intuitions as raw data against which theories are tested is misleading in the other direction as well. The method that actually operates is one of mutual adjustment. Principles are revised in the light of judgements about cases, and judgements about cases are revised in the light of principles that have earned our confidence elsewhere. Neither level has final authority, and the goal is a state in which the two support each other. Critics sometimes say that this is circular, and in a sense it is; but the circle is wide, and it is not obvious that any inquiry into how we should live could proceed in a straight line.

What follows is a modest but not trivial conclusion. Intuitions are neither oracles nor noise. The debunker who dismisses them all owes us an account of the standpoint from which the dismissal is made, and it is hard to find one that does not rely on some judgement of the same kind. The defender who treats them as data owes us something too: a willingness to let a strong theory overturn a widely shared reaction, as moral thought has done before, when the reaction turns out to rest on a feature of cases that should never have mattered.

passage: Among the records of past climate, ice cores enjoy a special prestige. Drilled from the great ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica, they contain small bubbles of air sealed off as snow was buried and compressed, so that a scientist can, in a sense, hold in a laboratory a sample of the atmosphere as it was long before any human being farmed. Tree rings, lake sediments and the shells of tiny marine organisms all have to be translated into climate through some chain of reasoning. The bubbles in ice seem to need no translation at all: the gas is simply there, waiting to be measured.

The appearance of directness is partly an illusion, and an instructive one. Snow does not seal itself the moment it falls. For decades or even centuries, depending on how quickly snow accumulates, the upper layer remains porous, and air from the surface continues to mix downward through it. By the time the bubbles finally close, the gas they hold is considerably younger than the ice that surrounds it. To date the air, then, researchers must model how compaction proceeds at a given site, which in turn depends on temperature and snowfall, the very quantities the core is being used to reconstruct. Temperature itself is not read off the ice but inferred from the proportions of heavier and lighter forms of water, a relationship calibrated against modern observations and assumed to have held in the past.

None of this makes the records untrustworthy. It does, however, change where their authority comes from. A core is persuasive not because it bypasses interpretation but because its interpretations can be checked against one another and against independent archives. Traces of very large volcanic eruptions, which can appear in cores drilled at opposite ends of the planet, allow records to be aligned; the timing of changes in ice can be compared with changes recorded in ocean sediments, whose dating rests on quite different assumptions. When such independent lines agree, the agreement is far harder to explain away than any single measurement, however direct it seems.

The point matters beyond the laboratory. Public arguments about climate often treat evidence as either raw and therefore reliable or interpreted and therefore suspect. Ice cores show why this division is unhelpful. Almost all scientific evidence is interpreted; what distinguishes strong evidence from weak is whether its interpretations are exposed to independent tests that could have failed. A measurement trusted because it seemed to speak for itself would deserve less confidence than one whose inferences had been stated openly and checked.
